title: Incident response for AI failures: when the assistant misbehaves live
hook: AI failures don't always throw an error; a model can be confidently wrong, so incident response needs a way to detect that, not just a crash to watch for.
inPlainWords: Because an AI system can fail by being confidently wrong instead of crashing, incident response needs monitoring on outcomes, not just uptime, plus a fast way to fall back to something safer.

useCase.title: The assistant starts giving a wrong refund amount, live
useCase.story: A provider-side model update silently changes behavior. For three hours, the assistant occasionally miscalculates refund amounts on a specific order type before anyone notices, because nothing crashed and no error was logged.

approaches.name: Wait for customer complaints to surface it
approaches.what: Rely on support tickets or reviews to reveal a problem.
approaches.avoidWhen: Always avoid relying on this alone, since it's slow and undercounts silent failures.
approaches.example: The miscalculation runs for three hours before the first complaint arrives.

approaches.name: Monitor outcome metrics, not just system health
approaches.what: Track business-level signals, like refund amounts issued, answer confidence and citation rate, alongside standard uptime and error-rate monitoring.
approaches.greatWhen: Always, for any AI feature with real consequences.
approaches.avoidWhen: Never skip; a "healthy" system with no crashes and low latency can still be confidently wrong.
approaches.example: A sudden jump in average refund amount triggers an alert with no error ever logged.

approaches.name: Have a kill switch or fallback ready
approaches.what: A fast way to disable the AI feature or fall back to a simpler, safer path, like a fixed rule or a human queue.
approaches.greatWhen: Always, prepared before an incident, not designed during one.
approaches.avoidWhen: Never skip preparing this in advance.
approaches.example: One flag reroutes refund calculation to the old, simple rule within seconds.

approaches.name: Run a blameless post-incident review
approaches.what: After the fact, document what happened, why detection was slow or fast, and what changes to make, without focusing on blaming an individual.
approaches.avoidWhen: Never skip; without it, the same failure mode repeats.
approaches.example: The write-up covers the timeline, the detection gap, and a follow-up task, with no names attached to blame.

approaches.name: Pre-define severity levels and an on-call path
approaches.what: Agree in advance what counts as a minor versus severe AI incident, and who gets paged for each.
approaches.greatWhen: Always, before the first real incident happens.
approaches.avoidWhen: Never improvise this during a live incident.
approaches.example: A wrong-refund pattern is pre-classified as severe, paging the on-call engineer automatically.

challenge.question: A provider-side model update causes wrong refund amounts for three hours, with no crash and no error logged, until a customer complains. What would have caught it sooner?

options.text: Monitoring outcome metrics like refund amounts and confidence, with an alert on unusual shifts, not just system health and error rates
options.why: The failure was confidently wrong, not crashed; only outcome-level monitoring would have flagged the unusual shift.

options.text: Waiting for more customer complaints to confirm the pattern
options.why: This is what happened, and it took three hours; it's not a detection method, it's the absence of one.
There was no error to threshold on; the system reported as healthy throughout.

options.text: Adding more logging detail to existing error logs
options.why: More detail helps investigate after the fact, but doesn't add detection for a failure that never triggers an error in the first place.

bestCase.title: Outcome monitoring catches a silent failure
bestCase.example: An alert fires when average refund amount shifts outside its normal range, 12 minutes after the provider update, letting the team switch to the fallback path before most customers are affected.

worstCase.title: Three hours of silent wrong answers
worstCase.example: No outcome monitoring exists. The first signal is a customer complaint three hours in, by which point hundreds of refunds may be affected, and the team has no fast way to disable the feature while they investigate.

route.travelling: A provider-side model update, live in production

steps.label: Update happens silently
steps.goes: The model provider updates behavior with no announcement.

steps.label: Outcome metrics shift
steps.goes: Average refund amount moves outside its normal range.

steps.label: Alert fires
steps.goes: The on-call engineer is paged within minutes.
steps.goesWrong: No outcome monitoring exists, so nothing fires until a customer complains three hours later.

steps.label: Flip the kill switch
steps.goes: The refund calculation falls back to the simpler, tested rule.

steps.label: Investigate the cause
steps.goes: The team traces it to the provider's silent update.

steps.label: Run a blameless review
steps.goes: Findings: add a canary check on provider updates, going forward.

takeaway: Monitor outcomes, not just uptime and errors, and have a fallback ready before the incident; a model can fail silently and confidently, with nothing to alert on unless you're watching the right thing.
